part2.intro: Three teenagers write about their dream home.
part2.question: For each question, choose the correct answer.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Lucas
texts.text: My dream home is a tree house in a forest. It would have one room with a big bed under the roof and a small kitchen with a fridge full of snacks. I'd climb up a ladder to get in, so my little sister couldn't follow me! There wouldn't be a TV, because I'd prefer to listen to the birds. I'd invite my best friend to stay at weekends.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Thao
texts.text: I'd love an apartment at the top of a tall building in the city centre. From the living room I'd see lights all over the city at night. I'd have a white sofa, a huge TV and a swimming pool on the roof. My grandparents would live in the flat downstairs, so I could visit them every day. I'd also need a lift – I hate stairs!

texts.label: C
texts.title: Ruby
texts.text: My perfect house would be by the sea, with big windows in every room. I'd have a garden full of flowers and vegetables, and a garage for my surfboards. The bathroom would have a shower outside, so I could wash after swimming. I'd paint every room a different colour. I don't want a big house – just enough space for me and lots of pets.

items.q: Who wants to live near family members?
Who would grow food at their home?
Who would not have a television?
Who would like to see a long way from their home at night?
Who wants a place to keep sports equipment?
Who wants a home that a family member can't get into?
Who says their home doesn't need to be large?

part3.title: Our summer in someone else's home
part3.text:
Last summer, thirteen-year-old Daniel Webb from Manchester spent four weeks living in someone else's home – in Spain! His family did a 'home swap' with the Ortega family from Valencia. The Webbs stayed in the Ortegas' apartment, and the Ortegas stayed in the Webbs' house.

"My mum found the idea on the internet," Daniel explains. "Hotels in Spain are expensive in August, and this way the holiday cost much less. We only paid for the plane tickets."

Before the swap, both families sent lots of emails and photos. "We had to tidy every room and make space in the cupboards for their clothes," says Daniel. "I wasn't happy about it, because I had to put all my things into boxes in the garage."

The Ortegas' apartment was on the eighth floor, near the beach. "It was smaller than our house, but it was really modern. There were fans in every room, which was great, because it was thirty-five degrees outside!" Daniel shared a bedroom with his younger brother. "That was the only bad thing. He talks in his sleep!"

The Ortegas loved Manchester too – even the rain. When they went home, they left a thank-you card and a big box of Spanish chocolates on the kitchen table.

"Now we send each other messages," says Daniel. "Their son Pablo is my age, and next summer he wants to come and stay with us in Manchester – at the same time as us!"

items.q: Why did Daniel's family decide to do a home swap?
options: It was cheaper than staying in a hotel.

items.q: How did Daniel feel about getting ready for the swap?
options: excited about meeting a new family
worried that his house was too small

items.q: What did Daniel like about the apartment in Spain?
options: It was bigger than his house.
He had his own bedroom there.

items.q: What did the Ortega family do before they left Manchester?
options: They left something for the Webbs.

items.q: What is Pablo planning to do?
options: move to England with his family
spend time with Daniel in Manchester

part4.title: Tiny houses
part4.text:
Tiny houses are becoming very popular in many countries. A tiny house is usually less than twenty square metres – about the {19} of one large bedroom! Many of them have wheels, so the owners can {20} them to a new place when they want.

How do people fit everything inside? Every piece of furniture has more than one use. A sofa can {21} into a bed at night, and there are cupboards under the stairs and shelves on every wall. The kitchen is usually small, and there is {22} room for a dining table, so people often eat on the sofa.

People who live in tiny houses say they {23} less money on heating and electricity. They also have fewer things, so cleaning the whole house only takes a few minutes!

But tiny houses are not for everyone. If you like having friends to stay, or you have a big family, you might find it difficult to {24} enough space for everyone.

part7.instruction: Look at the three pictures. Write the story shown in the pictures. Write 35 words or more.

pictures.caption: a boy alone at home cleaning the living room
the boy knocks a lamp off a table and it breaks on the floor
his parents come home and smile at the clean room while the boy shows them the broken lamp

part7.model: On Saturday, Tom's parents went shopping, so he decided to clean the house for them. He cleaned the kitchen and then started on the living room. But when he was cleaning the floor, he hit a table and the lamp fell and broke. When his parents came home, Tom told them about the lamp. They weren't angry because the house looked so clean!

items.q: Where does the girl's family live now?

script.t: Hi Jess! I heard you moved. Are you still in that flat above the café?
No, we left in March. Mum wanted to buy a flat by the river, but it was too expensive.
So where are you now?
We're renting a house on Green Lane. It's got a garden, so we can finally get a cat!

items.q: What does the boy need to buy for his bedroom?

script.t: Is your new bedroom ready, Daniel?
Nearly. My cousin gave me his old desk and chair, and Mum made some curtains for me.
So you've got everything?
Not quite. The light in the ceiling isn't very bright, so I need a lamp for my desk. I'm going to buy one on Saturday.

items.q: What time will the man come to repair the heating?

script.t: Hello, it's Mrs Carter. Our heating isn't working and the house is really cold. Could you come at half past eleven?
Sorry, I'm busy then. I've got another job at ten o'clock, but I could come before that. How about quarter to nine?
That's fine. My son leaves for school at half past eight, but I'll be at home.
Great. See you then.

items.q: Which is the boy's bedroom?

script.t: Is this your bedroom, Kai? The one with the big window?
No, that's my parents' room. Mine's at the end of the hall.
Oh, the one with the football posters?
That's my brother's. I'm in the small room with the bunk beds. My cousins sleep there with me when they visit.

items.q: What has the girl forgotten to bring?

script.t: Hi, Mrs Lee. I've brought my sleeping bag and my pillow for tonight.
Great, Amy. Did you bring a towel? We haven't got many clean ones.
Yes, it's in my bag.
Good. Have you got everything else?
Oh no! My toothbrush is still in the bathroom at home.

part2.intro: You will hear a woman leaving a message for a family who are going to stay in her holiday cottage.
part2.title: Holiday at Rose Cottage

items.label: Key: in a small box next to the
Switch for the heating is in the:

script.t: Hello, this is a message for the Wilson family. Welcome to Rose Cottage! I hope your journey was OK. I'm sorry I can't meet you today. The key isn't under the mat by the front door, like last year. I've put it in a small box next to the gate. The number to open the box is the same as the house number – twenty-two. The cottage has three bedrooms – two upstairs, and one small one downstairs, next to the bathroom. There are clean towels on every bed. It gets cold at night, even in summer, so you might need the heating. The switch isn't in the kitchen – it's in the garage, on the wall behind the door. If you need food, there's a shop in the village. It usually closes at six, but today's Sunday, so it closes at half past five. If you have any problems, please call me. My name's Mrs Penrose – that's P-E-N-R-O-S-E – and my phone number is on the fridge. Enjoy your stay!

part3.intro: You will hear Hoa talking to her friend Ben about staying at her aunt's apartment in London.

items.q: How long did Hoa stay in London?
Where did Hoa sleep?
options: in a small room near the kitchen

items.q: What did Hoa like best about the apartment?
What was the problem in the apartment?
options: The shower water got cold quickly.

items.q: What will Hoa do after school?

script.t: Hi Hoa! How was London? Were you there for two weeks?
We planned to stay for ten days, but Mum had to go back to work early, so it was only one week.
That's a shame. Where did you stay?

At my aunt's apartment. It only has two bedrooms. My cousin wanted me to share her room, but her bed is tiny. And the sofa in the living room was too short for me. So I slept in a little room next to the kitchen. That's usually where my aunt does her work.
Was there a good view? I know lots of apartments in London are near the river.

You can see the river from the kitchen window, but only a little. The kitchen's really modern too. But the best thing was the garden on the roof. There are lots of plants and a table, and we had breakfast up there every morning.
Amazing. Were there any problems?
Well, the lift was very slow, but it worked. The neighbours have a big dog, but it was always quiet. The worst thing was the shower – the hot water never lasted longer than two minutes!
Oh no! Did you take lots of pictures?
Hundreds! Come to my house after school and I'll show you. Mum wants to go back next summer, but we'll see.

items.intro: You will hear a girl talking to her father about her bedroom.
items.q: What does she want to change?

script.t: Dad, can I paint my bedroom this weekend? I'm bored of pink. I'd like green.
What about the carpet? It's very old. Shall we get a new one too?
No, the carpet's fine, and I love my furniture. It's just the walls. Please?
OK. Let's go and buy the paint tomorrow.

items.intro: You will hear a boy talking to a friend about his new neighbours.
items.q: What does he say about them?

script.t: We've got new neighbours next door. I was worried at first, because they've got three small kids. But they're really quiet! And yesterday they brought us a cake to say hello. They've invited us to their house for lunch on Saturday. Their garden's tiny, so we'll eat in the kitchen. They're lovely people.

items.intro: You will hear a woman on the radio talking about keeping your home warm in winter.
items.q: What is her advice?
options: Buy new heating for your home.
Close the curtains when it is dark.
Put a carpet in every room.

script.t: Lots of people think they need to spend money to keep their homes warm in winter. You don't need new heating or expensive carpets. Here's my best tip: when it gets dark, close your curtains. They stop the warm air from leaving through the windows. It's easy, and it's free!

items.intro: You will hear two friends talking about a birthday party.
items.q: Why can't the boy have the party at his house?
options: His grandmother is staying with them.

script.t: Are you having your birthday party at home, Leo?
I wanted to. Our living room's big enough, and Mum and Dad said they'd help. But my grandma's staying with us this month, and she isn't very well, so the house needs to be quiet.
Oh, I see.
So we're going to the bowling place in town instead.

part5.intro: You will hear Ryan talking to his friend Ella about his family's new house. Which room does each person like best?

script.t: So how's the new house, Ryan? Does everyone like it?
Yes, it's great. Mum thought she'd love the garden most, but she's always in the kitchen now. It's twice as big as our old one, and it's got a huge cooker.
And your dad?
He's got a garage for the first time, so he spends all weekend in there repairing his old bike.
What about your sister? I'm sure she's in her bedroom all the time.
Not really – Amy's bedroom is quite small. But the bathroom has a really big bath, and she stays in there for hours! None of us can get in.
Ha! And your grandpa lives with you, doesn't he?
Yes. We thought he'd like the dining room, because he loves big family dinners. But actually he's always outside in the garden, growing vegetables.
And you? Is your bedroom your favourite?
It's nice, but my favourite room is the living room. We've got a huge sofa and a big TV, so I watch football there with my friends.
What's the hall like? My mum says the houses on your street have really big halls.
It's big, but it's just a hall! There's nowhere to sit.
